title: Thinking with a document
excerpt: I started giving AI a document to read and update each run. The work improved, and writing things down helped me figure out what I was asking for.

sources.label: Rick's observation about documentation improving outputs across runs and agents, and article brief
Current shared collaboration principles: evidence, corrections, ownership, and original documents
Current Taskosaur work tracking and handoff guidance

intro: I started giving AI a file to read and update each time we worked. It held the brief, decisions we'd made, and corrections I wanted to keep. When I opened another session or switched agents, I pointed back to that file.

I found that the outputs got better across runs, including when I switched agents. I could put feedback somewhere the next agent would see it. Writing the feedback also made me work out what I actually wanted.

sections.heading: Getting past “this isn't quite right”
body: I can tell that a page isn't working before I can explain why. Asking an agent to improve it leaves a lot open to interpretation. Writing a brief makes me name the part I want to change.

On my portfolio's UI Systems Lab page, I wanted the prototype section to explain what the workspace enables. A list of what's in it wasn't the point. The Storybook patterns and the prototyping workspace let me work with the same ideas at different levels of fidelity.
That was a more useful direction than asking for better copy. Once it's written down, I can check a revision against it. I can also change my mind without losing track of the earlier decision.

evidence.note: Rick's Portfolio feedback explicitly asked for the prototypes section to focus on what the workspace enables and described it as the same Storybook patterns at a different fidelity. Reflection on writing remains for his review.
Supports distinguishing observations, assumptions, and unresolved decisions.

sections.heading: Keeping the correction
body: I can explain that direction in a chat and get a better revision. But if the correction stays in that conversation, another agent may start from the old brief.

Updating the document gives that feedback somewhere to go. The next run starts with the revised intent. Sometimes the update is a sentence; sometimes it's deleting an instruction that no longer makes sense. I don't need a new paragraph for every session.

evidence.note: The reported cross-run benefit is Rick's observation. His earlier Portfolio feedback explicitly shifted the prototypes section toward what the workspace enables.
Current guidance belongs at its owner; replace stale rules rather than accumulating instructions.

sections.heading: Taking it to another agent
body: I use Codex, Claude, Cursor, and Gemini. They don't share my conversation history. Giving them access to the same document lets me bring decisions from one tool into another.

I point them to the original rather than keeping a copy for each agent. Otherwise, I can fix one version and leave another out of date. I also ask the agent to read it; connecting a tool doesn't mean it has loaded the context.
They still interpret the brief differently. Having the same reference makes those differences easier to discuss. I can point to a decision and ask why the result departed from it.

evidence.note: The conversation establishes use of several agents and Rick's reported improvement across them.
Requires authoritative originals and truthful access claims; no automatic cross-tool memory is implied.

sections.heading: Reading what changed
body: I still have to read the edits. An agent can turn a tentative idea into a confident statement or drop a constraint during a rewrite. If I miss that, the next agent may treat it as something I've already agreed to.
The document helps me notice those changes. It also shows me where I haven't made a decision yet. I can leave a question open instead of accepting an answer just because it sounds finished.

evidence.note: Defines compact continuation context and meaningful checkpoints rather than transcript duplication.
Thinking benefits are reflective interpretation for Rick's review.

sections.heading: What I ask for each run
body: I ask the agent to read the current document before working, check what it changed, and update the parts that the next session will need. That includes unfinished work. If a check failed, I want the record to say so.
I keep the goal, constraints, decisions, and open questions. The chat can hold the rest. When several agents are working, they also need to check for each other's edits before saving.

evidence.note: Supports fresh orientation, verification, explicit unfinished work, and handoff checkpoints.
Requires preserving other writers' work and verifying claims.

sections.heading: Where it can go wrong
body: I haven't measured how much this helps, and a document can carry a mistake into the next run too. Old instructions and too much detail can make it harder to use. I have to revise it, not just keep adding to it.

What changes is the context I give the agent on the next run. The correction I made last time is there to read. So is the question I haven't answered yet. I can pick up either one without having to remember which chat it was in.

evidence.note: Qualitative personal experience only. No controlled benchmark, quantified gain, or guaranteed improvement is asserted.
Supports review, correction, and removal of stale guidance; document updates are context changes, not model training.
